stories.summary: Eleni and Dimitris visit the Museum of Greek Folk Musical Instruments in Plaka and explore traditional clarinets, lutes, and brass horns.
stories.narrative: Eleni and Dimitris visit the Museum of Greek Folk Musical Instruments in downtown Athens with adult chaperones. The educational exhibition displays how folk music originated centuries ago and was passed down through each generation. A helpful instructor gives the pupils a colourful brochure and detailed handouts about each traditional instrument. Dimitris looks at an antique wooden oboe and a rare wind pipe, while Eleni examines a handmade string violin used at a traditional island wedding. The guide explains the length of each tube and how artists play instrumental melodies without electric amplification. The excited children look forward to attending a live concert in the garden tonight.

stories.summary: Maya and Liam rehearse with their school rock band, writing lyrics, tuning guitars, and perfecting their drum rhythm.
stories.narrative: Maya and Liam are passionate members of a popular school rock band called The Camden Sparks. Every Tuesday, they meet in the music room to rehearse and compose. Maya is the lead vocal singer; she loves to write lyrics that inspire her friends, with catchy verses and a memorable chorus. Liam plays the electric guitar with dazzling speed, while Ben hits the percussion drum kit to establish a tight rhythm and steady beat. Their music teacher helped them register for the city music festival and make a hall reservation at a famous downtown venue. The band creates a rich melody and harmony, and is thrilled to perform on the main auditorium stage for their big annual performance.

stories.summary: George and Kelly learn how to manage their weekly pocket money, budget for expenses, and save up for a school charity project.
stories.narrative: George and Kelly receive a weekly pocket money allowance from their parents for helping with each household chore. In the past, Kelly would pester her mother for extra coins, simply to waste them on useless snacks and fancy toiletries. After studying how a smart consumer acts, the children decided to do intelligent research on financial habits. They learned that even a wealthy millionaire must track every bill and never owe money carelessly. Their parents provide three clear jars to organise their small income: one for essential needs, one for long-term savings, and one to donate. George managed to persuade Kelly to save approximately forty euros from every income source to buy school supplies for local children.

stories.student: Counselor Clara & The Big Bad Wolf
stories.summary: The Big Bad Wolf writes to the School Magazine problem page seeking advice on how to apologize, overcome prejudice, and join the forest orchestra.
stories.narrative: In a charming modern adaptation of an old fairy tale, the famous wolf sends a troubled letter to the school problem page. He writes about his misunderstood background: while villagers think he is frightening, he only loves playing the brass trumpet. Counselor Clara writes back with caring advice. She explains that if he apologises sincerely for past mistakes, people will forgive him and learn to trust him again. The wolf follows her guidance, holds an open rehearsal in the village square, and proves that mutual trust and music can turn a lonely wolf into a beloved friend.

grammar_lab.title: Inductive Grammar Lab: Modal Verbs (Ability, Obligation, Advice)
grammar_lab.subtitle: Discover how modal verbs express ability (can/could), obligation (must/have to), advice (should/ought to), and permission.
target_structures: Ability & Possibility: can / could / be able to
Obligation & Necessity: must / have to / need to
Lack of Necessity: don't have to / needn't
Advice & Suggestions: should / ought to / had better / why don't you

rules.structure: Ability: can / could / be able to
rules.use: Express general ability in present (can), past (could), or all tenses (be able to).
examples: He can play the trumpet with great skill.
When she was six, she could not read music notes.
With enough practice, you will be able to play in the school band.

rules.structure: Obligation & Necessity: must vs have to
rules.use: Express strong obligation from the speaker (must) or external rules/laws (have to).
examples: I must practice my violin every day to improve.
All students have to be at the rehearsal hall by 4:00 PM.

rules.structure: Prohibition vs No Obligation: mustn't vs don't have to
rules.use: Mustn't means it is forbidden. Don't have to means it is not necessary, but you may if you want.
examples: You mustn't touch the antique instruments in the glass display case.
You don't have to bring your own guitar; the school provides acoustic guitars.

rules.use: Give friendly guidance, recommendations, or constructive suggestions.
examples: You should make a weekly budget for your pocket money.
You ought to tune your guitar strings before going on stage.

practice_items.prompt: You _____ touch the antique folk instruments in the museum. It is strictly forbidden!
Tomorrow is Saturday! We _____ wake up early because there is no school.
practice_items.explanation: Don't have to expresses absence of obligation (it is not necessary).

practice_items.prompt: If you want to save pocket money, you _____ put a few coins in your piggy bank every week.
practice_items.explanation: Should is used to give sensible, constructive advice.

practice_items.prompt: Maya is very talented. She _____ sing beautifully and write catchy song lyrics.
Musicians _____ arrive at the concert venue thirty minutes before the show starts.
practice_items.explanation: Have to expresses an external requirement or rule.

practice_items.prompt: You look very tired from studying all night. Why _____ you take a short break?
practice_items.explanation: 'Why don't you...' is an idiomatic way to offer a friendly suggestion.

writing_workshop.title: Problem Letter & Advice Column
writing_workshop.prompt: Write a letter asking for advice about saving pocket money or practicing a musical instrument, OR write a reply from Counselor Clara giving friendly suggestions.
writing_workshop.model_text:
Dear Counselor Clara,

I have a problem and I really need your advice. Every week my parents give me a small pocket money allowance. However, by Tuesday I always spend all my coins on sweets and video games! Now our school band is planning a trip, and I cannot afford the ticket.

What should I do? How can I stop wasting my money?

Desperate Saver

---

Dear Desperate Saver,

Don't worry! Many students face the same challenge. Here is my advice:
First, you should keep a small notebook to record your daily expenses. When you see where your money goes, it is easier to make sensible choices.
Second, you ought to divide your allowance into jars: one for spending, and one for savings. Put your savings jar out of sight!
Third, you could ask your parents if you can do extra chores at home to earn a little extra income for the band trip.

Be patient, stick to your plan, and you will achieve your goal!

Best wishes,
Counselor Clara

scaffolding_steps.title: State the Problem Clearly
scaffolding_steps.tip: Explain who you are, what the situation is, and what worries you.

scaffolding_steps.title: Use Modal Verbs for Advice
scaffolding_steps.tip: Use 'You should...', 'You ought to...', 'Why don't you...', and 'You could...' to give polite guidance.

scaffolding_steps.title: Offer Practical Action Steps
scaffolding_steps.tip: Give two or three realistic ideas that the reader can try immediately.

scaffolding_steps.title: Encourage and Sign Off
scaffolding_steps.tip: End with a warm, encouraging closing sentence (e.g., 'Best wishes', 'Stay positive!').

checklist: I used greeting and sign-off formulas appropriate for an advice column.
